extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers of Kant)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Kant's criteria for making or evaluating judgements of taste (the aesthetic judgement of beauty) as discussed in the Critique of Judgement. Focuses on what constitutes a proper aesthetic judgement, how it differs from pleasantness and goodness, and the mental/state conditions that ground its claim to (subjective) universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness (entirely disinterested satisfaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging of an object or a method of representing it by an entirely disinterested satisfaction or dissatisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper judgement of taste must be disinterested: it must not be grounded in inclination, desire, usefulness, or any practical interest. Distinguish this from the Pleasant (which is tied to sensation and inclination) and the Good (which is tied to reason and will). Any interest—pathological (sensory) or practical (reason)—spoils the impartiality required for a judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective universal validity (universality without concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is that which apart from concepts is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one judges something beautiful, one implicitly claims that others ought to share the same satisfaction even though that claim is not based on concepts or objective cognition. This universality is 'subjective' or aesthetic (a claim to a 'universal voice'), not logical or conceptually demonstrable. The judgement imputes agreement to everyone without adducing conceptual reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among the Pleasant, the Beautiful, and the Good
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pleasant, the Beautiful, and the Good designate three different relations of representations to the feeling of pleasure and pain: that which gratifies is pleasant; that which pleases is beautiful; that which is esteemed or approved is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and apply these distinctions when evaluating responses to objects: the Pleasant is sensuous and linked to inclination (shared with animals), the Beautiful concerns a disinterested, contemplative pleasure unique to beings that are also rational, and the Good involves concepts and practical reason (value for the will). Examples: a spicy dish (pleasant), a flower's form (beautiful), health or moral worth (good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of purposiveness (purposiveness without purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste has nothing at its basis but the form of the purposiveness of an object (or of its mode of representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement rests on perceiving a form of purposiveness in an object's representation without attributing an objective or subjective purpose (no 'purpose' or practical end should ground the judgement). This 'purposiveness without purpose' is a formal feature of the representation that gives rise to the disinterested pleasure constitutive of aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free play of Imagination and Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of mind in the free play of the Imagination and the Understanding (so far as they agree with each other) is the subjective condition whose communicability underlies the judgement of taste; this harmony is the ground of the pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain aesthetic pleasure as arising from the felt harmony ('free play') between imagination (gathering manifold intuitions) and understanding (unity of representation). This harmonious, indeterminate activity is universally communicable and precedes the pleasurable feeling in a judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence of the judgement of taste over pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective universal communicability of the representation must be fundamental, and must have the pleasure in the object as its consequent; the judgement of taste (the claim of communicability) precedes the felt pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat pleasure as the primary; instead, the awareness that a representation is communicable (suitable for cognition-in-general via the free play of faculties) grounds the subsequent pleasure. If pleasure were prior and merely private, the claim to universality would collapse into mere pleasantness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of judgement (independence from charm and emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste on which charm and emotion have no influence (although they may be bound up with the satisfaction in the beautiful) is a pure judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure judgement excludes empirical admixtures—charm, sentimentality, and other emotions that derive from personal or contingent conditions. Anti-pattern: calling something beautiful because it moves you emotionally or because of particular charms; such admixtures undermine the universal claim of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure versus empirical aesthetical judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical judgements can be divided into empirical (material) and pure (formal). The empirical assert pleasantness or unpleasantness and belong to Sense; the pure assert beauty and are strictly judgements of Taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an aesthetic claim, distinguish whether it is material (based on sensation, contingent conditions, pleasure) or formal/pure (based on disinterested purposiveness of form). Only the latter carry the proper status of 'taste' in Kant's sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic universality is subjective, not logical (singular vs universal judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All judgements of taste are singular (aesthetic) judgements in logical quantity, yet they carry an aesthetical universality (validity for every one) that does not rest on concepts; transforming repeated singular judgements into a general concept yields a logical universal judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful distinguishing the logical form of a judgement from its aesthetic claim: 'This rose is beautiful' is an aesthetic singular that claims universal assent; 'Roses are beautiful' is a generalization (logical) built from repeated aesthetic judgements and no longer strictly an a priori aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: No subjective or objective purpose should determine the aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every purpose, if regarded as a ground of satisfaction, carries an interest; therefore no subjective purpose nor any representation of an objective purpose can be the determining ground of a judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid practical or moral justifications (concepts of the good) when making an aesthetic judgement. The judgement should not be cognitive (about the object's possibility or function) but concern only the relation of the representative powers—i.e., the form of purposiveness without purpose.
